metaDescription: Helping travellers manage money abroad with a faster, clearer, and more trustworthy mobile experience.

hero.title: TUI, Multi-Currency Travel Money
hero.summary: TUI's prepaid multi-currency travel card app hadn't been updated in years and no longer matched users' expectations of a modern financial product. I redesigned the experience to make managing travel money clearer and more trustworthy while retaining TUI's holiday-ready character.

blocks.html: TUI offers a prepaid Mastercard® that lets UK travellers hold and switch between up to 11 currencies. The existing app was built on legacy technology that could no longer support updates or new features, while its outdated design and unclear flows were eroding user confidence.

As Lead Product Designer, I led the end-to-end redesign across onboarding, navigation, card ordering, top-ups, currency conversion, balances, transactions, and card management, using competitive analysis and usability testing to validate the direction.

blocks.title: Business goals
items: Replace the legacy product with a modern, scalable experience
Bring the experience in line with modern fintech expectations
Improve acquisition at the travel-booking stage

blocks.title: Validation metrics
items: Task success across onboarding, top-ups, and currency conversion
User confidence after completing key tasks

items.challenge: Outdated interface and difficult navigation reduced confidence

items.goal: Monitor spending and exchange money efficiently
items.challenge: Exchange and fee information wasn't transparent or easy to find

blocks.html: The core tension: users who buy a TUI prepaid card need an app to manage it and monitor their spending. Many of these users first discover the app immediately after booking their holiday, making first impressions especially important. The challenge was balancing the trust and clarity expected from a financial product with the lightweight, enjoyable experience users associate with travel.
Research combined stakeholder workshops, competitive benchmarking, and usability testing of the live product to identify the highest-friction journeys.

items.finding: Onboarding was confusing, and essential card controls were missing from the app.
items.insight: Simplify card setup and bring everyday card management into the app.

items.finding: Hidden navigation and fragmented account information made money management difficult.
items.insight: Bring balances, wallets, and key actions into a clearer structure.

items.finding: Top-up and conversion flows felt too technical, with fees and exchange rates hard to find.
items.insight: Turn them into guided flows with rates, fees, and amounts shown upfront.

blocks.html: The hardest tradeoff was balancing banking-grade clarity against a travel-friendly, lightweight feel — leaning too far toward either risked feeling either untrustworthy or overly clinical.

The experience adapts from the start based on whether users already have a TUI prepaid card. Existing cardholders can link their card and continue, while new users are guided seamlessly into ordering one. Once set up, everyday card controls stay within easy reach, from viewing card details and PIN to freezing a card or blocking and ordering a replacement.

The home screen provides an aggregated balance and transaction history across currencies, while dedicated wallets show currency-specific activity. Users can customise how wallets are displayed and personalise them with travel photos, bringing TUI's leisure feel into everyday money management.

Users can top up directly from a regular bank card or convert money between existing currency balances, with clear amounts and exchange rates throughout the flow so they always understand where their money is coming from and where it's going.

The redesigned app launched in September 2025, replacing the previous version entirely. Usability testing showed improvements across the core journeys, particularly onboarding, where the previous experience had seen the most significant drop-off.

blocks.html: The redesigned experience delivers a more cohesive mobile product across iOS and Android. Users can now manage multiple currency wallets, review transactions by currency, top up more efficiently, convert money with greater confidence, and add their travel card to Apple Pay or Google Wallet for everyday spending.
What is externally visible is store feedback, and it splits into three distinct causes:

items.html: Design reception is positive where evaluated — layout, clarity, and tone match pre-launch usability testing.

Most login complaints trace to an onboarding communication gap, not a defect. The new app runs on a separate system from both the old app and a legacy web portal that remained live; old credentials don't carry over, and users must fully re-register. This wasn't communicated clearly, so users who could still log into the old web portal saw the new app reject the same credentials — reading as a bug when it's the expected result of two disconnected systems.
One genuine technical bug did surface: the app is case-sensitive, and some phones auto-capitalize the first character typed, silently altering the password as it's entered.

blocks.html: What looked like one wave of technical failures was actually two problems with different owners: the account-migration confusion is an onboarding-communication gap, closer to my domain than engineering's, while the case-sensitivity bug and other data/QA issues are genuinely technical. Launching a full replacement app leaves no soft landing for either kind — users don't separate "unclear messaging" from "broken app," they just leave a low rating.

The lesson: onboarding communication for a full system replacement needs the same validation rigor as the interface itself, especially with a legacy system still live in parallel. Next step is clarifying the re-registration messaging, fixing the case-sensitivity bug, and re-running usability testing to isolate design feedback more cleanly.
